claim: Centrosomes comprise a pair of centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).
source: Centrosomes comprise a pair of centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM).
evidence: This is a well-established definition of centrosome structure that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The PCM expands dramatically as cells enter mitosis.
source: The PCM expands dramatically as cells enter mitosis, but it is unclear how this occurs.
evidence: This is a well-documented phenomenon in cell biology supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The centriole protein Asl initiates the recruitment of DSpd-2 and Cnn to mother centrioles.
source: In this study, we show that the centriole protein Asl initiates the recruitment of DSpd-2 and Cnn to mother centrioles
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including antibody injection experiments (Figure 5) and FRAP experiments (Figure 4).

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn assemble into co-dependent scaffold-like structures that spread outwards from the mother centriole.
source: both proteins then assemble into co-dependent scaffold-like structures that spread outwards from the mother centriole and recruit most, if not all, other PCM components.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments showing inside-out assembly (Figures 1, 2, 4) and 3D-SIM imaging (Figure 3).

claim: In the absence of either DSpd-2 or Cnn, mitotic PCM assembly is diminished.
source: In the absence of either DSpd-2 or Cnn, mitotic PCM assembly is diminished
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of PCM protein levels in larval brain cells lacking either protein (Figure 9B, C).

claim: In the absence of both DSpd-2 and Cnn, mitotic PCM assembly appears to be abolished.
source: in the absence of both proteins, it appears to be abolished.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that mitotic PCM levels do not rise above interphase levels in double mutants (Figure 9D, H).

claim: DSpd-2 helps incorporate Cnn into the PCM.
source: We show that DSpd-2 helps incorporate Cnn into the PCM
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced Cnn levels at centrosomes in the absence of DSpd-2 (Figure 7) and FRAP experiments (Figure 4).

claim: Cnn helps maintain DSpd-2 within the PCM.
source: Cnn then helps maintain DSpd-2 within the PCM
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments showing that DSpd-2 incorporation rate is normal in cnn mutants but DSpd-2 levels are reduced (Figure 8).

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn create a positive feedback loop that promotes robust PCM expansion around the mother centriole during mitosis.
source: creating a positive feedback loop that promotes robust PCM expansion around the mother centriole during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutual dependence of DSpd-2 and Cnn for their centrosomal localization and maintenance (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Centrosomes help regulate many cell processes, including cell shape, cell polarity, and cell division.
source: Centrosomes help regulate many cell processes, including cell shape, cell polarity, and cell division (Doxsey et al., 2005; Bettencourt-Dias and Glover, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrosome defects have been implicated in several human pathologies.
source: centrosome defects have been implicated in several human pathologies (Nigg and Raff, 2009; Zyss and Gergely, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrosomes are the major microtubule-organising centres in many animal cells.
source: Centrosomes are the major microtubule (MT)-organising centres (MTOCs) in many animal cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Several hundred proteins are concentrated in the PCM.
source: Several hundred proteins are concentrated in the PCM, including many MT-organising proteins, cell-cycle regulators, and checkpoint and signalling proteins (Müller et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Centrioles organize only small amounts of PCM in interphase cells.
source: Although centrioles usually organize only small amounts of PCM in interphase cells, the PCM expands dramatically as cells prepare to enter mitosis
evidence: This is established knowledge about centrosome behavior during the cell cycle.

claim: Centrosome maturation is the process by which PCM expands dramatically as cells prepare to enter mitosis.
source: the PCM expands dramatically as cells prepare to enter mitosis—a process termed centrosome maturation (Khodjakov and Rieder, 1999).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Asl/Cep152 has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: These include (1) centriole-associated proteins, such as 'Asl/Cep152' (Bonaccorsi et al., 1998; Varmark et al., 2007; Dzhindzhev et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sas-4/CPAP has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: These include (1) centriole-associated proteins, such as 'Asl/Cep152' (Bonaccorsi et al., 1998; Varmark et al., 2007; Dzhindzhev et al., 2010) and 'Sas-4/CPAP' (Cho et al., 2006; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pericentrin/D-PLP has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: proteins that have a centriole-associated fraction and a fraction that spreads out into the PCM, such as 'Pericentrin/D-PLP' (Martinez-Campos et al., 2004; Zimmerman et al., 2004; Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DSpd-2/Cep192 has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: 'DSpd-2/Cep192' (Pelletier et al., 2004; Dix and Raff, 2007; Gomez-Ferreria et al., 2007; Giansanti et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2008; Joukov et al., 2010; Decker et al., 2011; Joukov et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cnn/Cdk5Rap2 has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: proteins that reside in the PCM, such as 'Cnn/Cdk5Rap2' (Megraw et al., 1999; Lucas and Raff, 2007; Fong et al., 2008; Barr et al., 2010; Conduit et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DGp71WD/NEDD1 has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: 'DGp71WD/NEDD1' (Haren et al., 2006, 2009; Lüders et al., 2006; Manning et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: γ-tubulin has been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: and 'γ-tubulin' (Sunkel et al., 1995; Hannak et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polo/Plk1 and Aurora A mitotic protein kinases have been implicated in mitotic PCM assembly.
source: mitotic protein kinases, such as 'Polo/Plk1' and 'Aurora A' (Barr and Gergely, 2007; Petronczki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In super-resolution microscopy studies, several PCM proteins appeared to be highly organized around interphase centrioles.
source: In recent super-resolution microscopy studies, several of these proteins appeared to be highly organized around interphase centrioles, but the organisation of proteins within the extended mitotic PCM was much less apparent (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The organisation of proteins within the extended mitotic PCM was much less apparent in super-resolution microscopy studies.
source: In recent super-resolution microscopy studies, several of these proteins appeared to be highly organized around interphase centrioles, but the organisation of proteins within the extended mitotic PCM was much less apparent (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mitotic PCM is assembled on an underlying scaffold structure.
source: It has long been thought that the mitotic PCM is assembled on an underlying scaffold structure (Dictenberg et al., 1998; Schnackenberg et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila Centrosomin (Cnn) can form a scaffold around centrioles.
source: We recently showed that Drosophila Centrosomin (Cnn) can form such a scaffold around centrioles and that this scaffold is assembled from the inside out (Conduit et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Cnn scaffold is assembled from the inside out.
source: We recently showed that Drosophila Centrosomin (Cnn) can form such a scaffold around centrioles and that this scaffold is assembled from the inside out (Conduit et al., 2014): Cnn molecules continuously incorporate into the scaffold around the centrioles and the scaffold then fluxes slowly outward, away from the centrioles.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Cnn molecules continuously incorporate into the scaffold around the centrioles and the scaffold then fluxes slowly outward, away from the centrioles.
source: Cnn molecules continuously incorporate into the scaffold around the centrioles and the scaffold then fluxes slowly outward, away from the centrioles.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript (Conduit et al., 2014).

claim: Many PCM proteins can be recruited to mitotic centrosomes in the absence of Cnn, albeit at reduced levels.
source: Many PCM proteins, however, can be recruited to mitotic centrosomes in the absence of Cnn, albeit at reduced levels (Lucas and Raff, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: At least one other protein besides Cnn must be able to form a scaffold around centrioles that can recruit other PCM components.
source: Many PCM proteins, however, can be recruited to mitotic centrosomes in the absence of Cnn, albeit at reduced levels (Lucas and Raff, 2007), suggesting that at least one other protein must be able to form a scaffold around centrioles that can recruit other PCM components.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PCM proteins can still be recruited without Cnn.

claim: Asl-GFP and DSas-4-GFP are closely associated with centrioles.
source: Asl-GFP and DSas-4-GFP are known to be closely associated with centrioles (Fu and Glover, 2012; Mennella et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Asl-GFP and DSas-4-GFP fusions were tightly localized in the centre of the PCM.
source: their fusions were tightly localized in the centre of the PCM; they exhibited a fluorescence intensity profile similar to that of sub-resolution (170 nm) beads (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The true distribution of Asl-GFP and DSas-4-GFP was below the resolution of the microscope system used.
source: they exhibited a fluorescence intensity profile similar to that of sub-resolution (170 nm) beads (Figure 1A), indicating that their true distribution was below the resolution of our microscope system.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with sub-resolution beads in Figure 1A.

claim: Asl-GFP, Sas-4-GFP, AurA-GFP, DGp71WD-GFP, γ-tubulin-GFP, and Polo-GFP fluorescence all recovered evenly throughout the domain that each protein originally occupied after photobleaching.
source: After photobleaching, the Asl-GFP, Sas-4-GFP, AurA-GFP, DGp71WD-GFP, γ-tubulin-GFP, and Polo-GFP fluorescence all recovered at different rates, but each protein appeared to recover evenly throughout the domain that it originally occupied (Figure 1B,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Video 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Most PCM proteins are recruited to centrosomes by binding sites that are already distributed throughout the PCM volume that each protein occupies.
source: We conclude that most PCM proteins are recruited to centrosomes by binding sites that are already distributed throughout the PCM volume that each protein occupies (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is inferred from the even recovery pattern observed in FRAP experiments.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence initially recovered only in the central region of the PCM and then gradually began to recover in the more peripheral regions after photobleaching.
source: Unlike the other PCM components we tested, DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence initially recovered only in the central region of the PCM and then gradually began to recover in the more peripheral regions (Figure 1C,F,G; Video 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DSpd-2 is recruited to binding sites that are only located close to the centrioles.
source: This suggested that, like Cnn (Conduit et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2M,N), DSpd-2 is recruited to binding sites that are only located close to the centrioles
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP recovery pattern of DSpd-2-GFP.

claim: Once released from binding sites close to centrioles, DSpd-2 spreads slowly outward into the more peripheral regions of the PCM.
source: once released from these sites, it then spreads slowly outward into the more peripheral regions of the PCM (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP recovery pattern of DSpd-2-GFP.

claim: The central region of DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence exhibited a typical, logarithmic-shaped, FRAP recovery curve, with a fast initial recovery rate that gradually slowed over time.
source: The central region of DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence exhibited a typical, logarithmic-shaped, FRAP recovery curve, with a fast initial recovery rate that gradually slowed over time (green line, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The peripheral regions of DSpd-2-GFP exhibited an unusual FRAP recovery curve, with a slow initial recovery rate that gradually increased over time.
source: In contrast, the peripheral regions exhibited an unusual FRAP recovery curve, with a slow initial recovery rate that gradually increased over time (solid red line, Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP molecules are constantly moving from the centre of the centrosome to the periphery.
source: These unusual recovery dynamics at the periphery of the PCM can most easily be explained if DSpd-2-GFP molecules are constantly moving from the centre of the centrosome to the periphery
evidence: This is inferred from the unusual peripheral recovery kinetics observed in FRAP experiments.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP has a similar distribution to GFP-Cnn with several spoke-like projections extending from a central ring.
source: DSpd-2-GFP had a similar distribution with several spoke-like projections extending from a central ring (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Much less DSpd-2 extended into the more peripheral regions of the PCM compared to Cnn.
source: although, in agreement with our radial profiling data, much less DSpd-2 extended into the more peripheral regions of the PCM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP and mCherry-Cnn extensively overlapped in the more central regions of the PCM.
source: Two-colour 3D-SIM in living embryos confirmed that DSpd-2-GFP and mCherry-Cnn extensively overlapped in the more central regions of the PCM (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by two-color 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The more peripheral Cnn projections usually contained small amounts of DSpd-2.
source: revealed that the more peripheral Cnn projections usually contained small amounts of DSpd-2 (arrowheads, Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by two-color 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The GFP-Cnn projections were no longer visible when the MTs were depolymerized with colchicine.
source: Unsurprisingly, the GFP–Cnn projections (Figure 3A) were no longer visible when the MTs were depolymerized with colchicine, and the GFP–Cnn scaffold became more compact and amorphous in appearance (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data after colchicine treatment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The small amounts of DSpd-2 extending into the peripheral PCM were lost when the MTs were depolymerized.
source: The small amounts of DSpd-2 extending into the peripheral PCM (Figure 3C) were also lost when the MTs were depolymerized (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data after colchicine treatment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The more central DSpd-2-GFP region retained a clear organisation with several spoke-like projections emanating outward from a central ring when MTs were depolymerized.
source: but the more central DSpd-2-GFP region retained a clear organisation, with several spoke-like projections of DSpd-2-GFP emanating outward into the PCM from a central ring (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data after colchicine treatment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP is part of a scaffold-like structure that forms around the centrioles and retains some macromolecular structural integrity even in the absence of MTs.
source: We conclude that DSpd-2-GFP is part of a scaffold-like structure that forms around the centrioles and that retains some macromolecular structural integrity even in the absence of MTs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DSpd-2 structure persists after MT depolymerization.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn both seemed to emanate from a single toroidal structure that contains the mother centriole.
source: In our 3D-SIM images, we noticed that DSpd-2 and, to a lesser extent, Cnn both seemed to emanate from a single toroidal structure that we presume contains the mother centriole (arrows, Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is observed in 3D-SIM images shown in Figure 3.

claim: After photobleaching, DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence initially recovered in a toroidal pattern and then moved slowly outwards on dynamic projections.
source: This analysis revealed that after photobleaching DSpd-2-GFP fluorescence initially recovered in a toroidal pattern (t = 30 s, Figure 4A) and then moved slowly outwards on dynamic projections (t = 120 s to t = 450 s, Figure 4A; Video 2A).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM FRAP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The initial toroidal distribution of recovering DSpd-2-GFP was very similar to that of Asl, which forms a toroid specifically around the mother centriole.
source: The initial toroidal distribution was very similar to that previously reported for Asl, one of the several proteins that form a toroid specifically around the mother centriole (Mennella et al., 2013) (compare the recovering DSpd-2-GFP signal at t = 30 s in Figure 4A to the unbleached Asl-GFP signal shown in the inset; also compare the average profile of Asl-GFP to the average initial recovery profile of DSpd-2-GFP, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of 3D-SIM FRAP data with Asl distribution shown in Figure 4.

claim: DSpd-2-GFP is initially incorporated into the PCM by binding sites that are tightly concentrated around only one of the two centrioles—almost certainly the mother.
source: Thus, DSpd-2-GFP is initially incorporated into the PCM by binding sites that are tightly concentrated around only one of the two centrioles—almost certainly the mother—and the spatial distribution of these sites extensively overlaps with the distribution of Asl.
evidence: This is inferred from the toroidal recovery pattern matching Asl distribution.

claim: The spatial distribution of DSpd-2 binding sites extensively overlaps with the distribution of Asl.
source: Thus, DSpd-2-GFP is initially incorporated into the PCM by binding sites that are tightly concentrated around only one of the two centrioles—almost certainly the mother—and the spatial distribution of these sites extensively overlaps with the distribution of Asl.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of recovery patterns in Figure 4C.

claim: GFP-Cnn fluorescence initially recovered in a broader region around the centrioles than DSpd-2-GFP.
source: when we performed 3D-SIM FRAP with GFP-Cnn, the fluorescence initially recovered in the central region of the PCM (t = 60 s, Figure 4B), but this region was significantly broader than the toroidal region in which DSpd-2-GFP initially recovered (see t = 30 s, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM FRAP data comparing Cnn and DSpd-2 shown in Figure 4.

claim: Centrosomal GFP-Cnn fluorescence recovered more slowly than that of DSpd-2-GFP.
source: Moreover, centrosomal GFP-Cnn fluorescence recovered more slowly than that of DSpd-2-GFP (compare Figure 1F to Figure 1—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of FRAP recovery rates shown in Figure 1.

claim: The centrosomal binding sites for DSpd-2 and Cnn appear to be concentrated around the mother centriole but do not precisely overlap.
source: Thus, although the centrosomal binding sites for DSpd-2 and Cnn appear to be concentrated around the mother centriole, they do not precisely overlap and they recruit DSpd-2 and Cnn at different rates
evidence: This is inferred from the different recovery patterns and rates observed in FRAP experiments.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn are not incorporated into the PCM together as part of the same complex.
source: strongly suggesting that DSpd-2 and Cnn are not incorporated into the PCM together as part of the same complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the different spatial and temporal patterns of incorporation.

claim: Anti-Asl antibodies reduced the rate of DSpd-2-GFP incorporation into the PCM by approximately 75%.
source: Anti-Asl antibodies bound to centrosomes and reduced the rate of DSpd-2-GFP incorporation into the PCM by ∼75%, whereas anti-DSas-4 and anti-D-PLP antibodies had little effect (Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by antibody injection FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Anti-DSas-4 and anti-D-PLP antibodies had little effect on DSpd-2-GFP incorporation into the PCM.
source: Anti-Asl antibodies bound to centrosomes and reduced the rate of DSpd-2-GFP incorporation into the PCM by ∼75%, whereas anti-DSas-4 and anti-D-PLP antibodies had little effect (Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by antibody injection FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Asl is required for the centrosomal localization of DSpd-2.
source: These observations are consistent with the previous finding that Asl is required for the centrosomal localization of DSpd-2 (Giansanti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and consistent with current experimental data.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed several strong direct interactions between Asl and DSpd-2.
source: Moreover, our yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) analysis revealed several strong direct interactions between Asl and DSpd-2 (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Asl has an important, and potentially direct, role in recruiting DSpd-2 to mother centrioles in fly embryos.
source: Although we cannot be certain that Asl and DSpd-2 interact directly in vivo, collectively our data indicate that Asl has an important, and potentially direct, role in recruiting DSpd-2 to mother centrioles in fly embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including antibody inhibition and Y2H data.

claim: Anti-DSpd-2 antibodies inhibit the rate of Cnn incorporation into the PCM by approximately 75%.
source: We previously showed that anti-DSpd-2 or anti-Asl antibodies, but not anti-D-PLP or anti-Sas-4 antibodies, inhibit the rate of Cnn incorporation into the PCM by ∼75% and ∼55%, respectively, suggesting that both DSpd-2 and Asl may have a role in recruiting Cnn to centrosomes (Conduit et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Anti-Asl antibodies inhibit the rate of Cnn incorporation into the PCM by approximately 55%.
source: We previously showed that anti-DSpd-2 or anti-Asl antibodies, but not anti-D-PLP or anti-Sas-4 antibodies, inhibit the rate of Cnn incorporation into the PCM by ∼75% and ∼55%, respectively, suggesting that both DSpd-2 and Asl may have a role in recruiting Cnn to centrosomes (Conduit et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The distribution of DSpd-2-GFP around the mother centriole closely matched the distribution of the initial binding sites for GFP-Cnn.
source: We noticed, however, that the distribution of DSpd-2-GFP, but not Asl-GFP, around the mother centriole closely matched the distribution of the initial binding sites for GFP-Cnn, as revealed by our 3D-SIM FRAP experiments (compare the recovering GFP-Cnn signal at t = 60 s in Figure 4B to the unbleached DSpd-2-GFP signal at t = −30 s in Figure 4A; also compare the average profile of DSpd-2-GFP to the average initial recovery profile of GFP-Cnn, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of 3D-SIM FRAP data shown in Figure 4.

claim: DSpd-2 may provide the major centrosomal binding site for Cnn in embryos.
source: This suggests that DSpd-2 may provide the major centrosomal binding site for Cnn in embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial overlap of DSpd-2 and Cnn initial binding sites.

claim: The amount of Cnn localized to centrosomes in eggs was reduced by approximately 80% in the absence of DSpd-2.
source: In support of this possibility, we found that the amount of Cnn localized to centrosomes in eggs was reduced by ∼80% in the absence of DSpd-2 (Figure 7)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The centrosomal localization of Cnn is perturbed in dspd-2 mutant brain cells.
source: consistent with previous reports that the centrosomal localization of Cnn is perturbed in dspd-2 mutant brain cells (Dix and Raff 2007; Giansanti et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed several strong direct interactions between DSpd-2 and Cnn.
source: Moreover, our Y2H analysis revealed several strong direct interactions between DSpd-2 and Cnn but only one, much weaker, direct interaction between Cnn and Asl (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid analysis revealed only one, much weaker, direct interaction between Cnn and Asl.
source: Moreover, our Y2H analysis revealed several strong direct interactions between DSpd-2 and Cnn but only one, much weaker, direct interaction between Cnn and Asl (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DSpd-2 has an important, and potentially direct, role in recruiting Cnn to mother centrioles in fly embryos.
source: Although we cannot be certain that Cnn and DSpd-2 interact directly in vivo, collectively our data indicate that DSpd-2 has an important, and potentially direct, role in recruiting Cnn to mother centrioles in fly embryos, while Asl appears to have a more minor role.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including localization dependence and Y2H data.

claim: Asl appears to have a more minor role in recruiting Cnn to mother centrioles compared to DSpd-2.
source: Although we cannot be certain that Cnn and DSpd-2 interact directly in vivo, collectively our data indicate that DSpd-2 has an important, and potentially direct, role in recruiting Cnn to mother centrioles in fly embryos, while Asl appears to have a more minor role.
evidence: This is inferred from the weaker Y2H interaction and smaller effect on Cnn recruitment.

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the amount of DSpd-2-GFP associated with centrosomes in the absence of Cnn.
source: Although there was a dramatic reduction in the amount of DSpd-2-GFP associated with centrosomes in the absence of Cnn (Figure 8A,B)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: The initial rate of DSpd-2-GFP incorporation was unperturbed in cnn mutant embryos.
source: FRAP experiments revealed that the initial rate of DSpd-2-GFP incorporation was unperturbed (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: The localization of Asl-GFP was largely unperturbed in cnn mutant embryos.
source: The localization of Asl-GFP (which appears to recruit DSpd-2) was also largely unperturbed in cnn mutant embryos (Figure 8F,G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8F,G.

claim: The residual DSpd-2-GFP appeared to be more tightly associated with the centrioles in the absence of Cnn.
source: The residual DSpd-2-GFP appeared to be more tightly associated with the centrioles in the absence of Cnn (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is observed in imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The PCM fraction of DSpd-2 moved rapidly away from the centrioles in small 'flares' in the absence of Cnn.
source: while the PCM fraction of the protein moved rapidly away from the centrioles in small 'flares' (Video 4).
evidence: This is observed in video data (Video 4).

claim: Cnn is not required for the initial incorporation of DSpd-2 into the PCM, but is required for the proper maintenance of DSpd-2 within the PCM.
source: These observations suggest that Cnn is not required for the initial incorporation of DSpd-2 into the PCM, but is required for the proper maintenance of DSpd-2 within the PCM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that incorporation rate is normal but total levels are reduced in cnn mutants.

claim: Centrosome maturation in mitotic brain cells that lacked either Cnn or DSpd-2 was perturbed, but not abolished.
source: As shown previously, centrosome maturation in mitotic brain cells that lacked either Cnn (Megraw et al., 2001; Lucas and Raff, 2007) or DSpd-2 (Dix and Raff, 2007; Giansanti et al., 2008) was perturbed, but not abolished, and mitotic centrosomes organized levels of PCM that were significantly above those observed in interphase cells (Figure 9B,C,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9 and citations to previous literature.

claim: Centrosome maturation appeared to be abolished in the mitotic brain cells lacking both Cnn and DSpd-2.
source: Remarkably, however, centrosome maturation appeared to be abolished in the mitotic brain cells lacking both Cnn and DSpd-2 (Figure 9D,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 9D,H.

claim: Centrosomes in mitotic cells lacking either Cnn or DSpd-2 that also lacked D-TACC could still partially mature.
source: This effect was specific to the loss of both Cnn and DSpd-2, as centrosomes in mitotic cells lacking either Cnn or DSpd-2 that also lacked the abundant PCM protein D-TACC could still partially mature (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most PCM proteins appear to rely on Cnn and DSpd-2 for their recruitment to mitotic centrosomes.
source: Thus, most PCM proteins appear to rely on Cnn and DSpd-2 for their recruitment to mitotic centrosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PCM assembly is abolished in the double mutant.

claim: In fixed prophase cells, centrosomal asters were detectable in 100% of WT cells.
source: In fixed prophase cells (when centrosomal MT asters are most prominent), centrosomal asters were detectable in 100% of WT cells (Figure 9I; n = 11)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fixed cells shown in Figure 9I.

claim: In fixed prophase cells, centrosomal asters were detectable in 55% of cells lacking Cnn.
source: 55% of cells lacking Cnn (Figure 9J; n = 58)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fixed cells shown in Figure 9J.

claim: In fixed prophase cells, centrosomal asters were detectable in 57% of cells lacking DSpd-2.
source: 57% of cells lacking DSpd-2 (Figure 9K; n = 14)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fixed cells shown in Figure 9K.

claim: In fixed prophase cells, centrosomal asters were detectable in 0% of cells lacking both Cnn and DSpd-2.
source: but in 0% of cells lacking both proteins (Figure 9L; n = 15).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of fixed cells shown in Figure 9L.

claim: In live mitotic brain cells, centrosomes with MT asters were detectable in almost all cells lacking either Cnn (n = 18/18) or DSpd-2 (n = 24/25).
source: In live mitotic brain cells co-expressing the centriolar marker GFP-PACT and the MT marker Jupiter-mCherry (Figure 9—figure supplement 2; Video 5), centrosomes with MT asters were detectable in almost all cells lacking either Cnn (n = 18/18) or DSpd-2 (n = 24/25)
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2 and Video 5.

claim: In live mitotic brain cells, centrosomes with MT asters were detectable in almost no cells lacking both Cnn and DSpd-2 (n = 1/24).
source: but in almost no cells lacking both proteins (n = 1/24).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data.

claim: Cells lacking both DSpd-2 and Cnn are unable to assemble centrosomal MTOCs during mitosis.
source: We conclude that cells lacking both DSpd-2 and Cnn are unable to assemble centrosomal MTOCs during mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of MT asters in double mutant cells.

claim: The assembly of the mitotic PCM in flies appears to depend on just two proteins, Cnn and DSpd-2.
source: Remarkably, we show here that the assembly of the mitotic PCM in flies appears to depend on just two proteins, Cnn and DSpd-2.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn form scaffolds that initially assemble around the mother centriole and then spread outward.
source: Both proteins appear to form scaffolds that initially assemble around the mother centriole and then spread outward, forming a dynamic platform upon which most, if not all, other PCM proteins ultimately assemble.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP and 3D-SIM imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn form a dynamic platform upon which most, if not all, other PCM proteins ultimately assemble.
source: Both proteins appear to form scaffolds that initially assemble around the mother centriole and then spread outward, forming a dynamic platform upon which most, if not all, other PCM proteins ultimately assemble.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PCM assembly is abolished without both proteins.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn partially depend on each other for their centrosomal localization.
source: DSpd-2 and Cnn partially depend on each other for their centrosomal localization, and both proteins are required to ensure robust centrosome maturation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced levels of each protein in the absence of the other (Figures 7, 8).

claim: Both DSpd-2 and Cnn are required to ensure robust centrosome maturation.
source: DSpd-2 and Cnn partially depend on each other for their centrosomal localization, and both proteins are required to ensure robust centrosome maturation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced PCM assembly in single mutants (Figure 9B, C).

claim: In the absence of one of DSpd-2 or Cnn, reduced levels of the other protein still localize around the centrioles and can support the partial assembly of the mitotic PCM.
source: In the absence of one of these proteins, reduced levels of the other protein still localize around the centrioles and can support the partial assembly of the mitotic PCM.
evidence: This is supported by data from single mutant analysis (Figures 7, 8, 9).

claim: In fly embryos, Asl initially helps recruit DSpd-2 to centrioles and DSpd-2 then helps to recruit Cnn.
source: Our results strongly suggest that in fly embryos Asl initially helps recruit DSpd-2 to centrioles and DSpd-2 then helps to recruit Cnn.
evidence: This is supported by antibody inhibition experiments (Figure 5) and localization dependencies (Figures 4, 7).

claim: Cnn does not appear to be required to recruit either Asl or DSpd-2 to centrosomes.
source: Cnn does not appear to be required to recruit either Asl or DSpd-2 to centrosomes, but it is required to properly maintain DSpd-2 within the PCM.
evidence: This is supported by data showing normal Asl and DSpd-2 incorporation rates in cnn mutants (Figure 8).

claim: Cnn is required to properly maintain DSpd-2 within the PCM.
source: Cnn does not appear to be required to recruit either Asl or DSpd-2 to centrosomes, but it is required to properly maintain DSpd-2 within the PCM.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data showing normal incorporation but reduced steady-state levels (Figure 8).

claim: The interaction between DSpd-2 and Cnn creates a positive feedback loop that drives the dramatic expansion of the PCM scaffold around mother centrioles during mitosis.
source: We speculate that this interaction between DSpd-2 and Cnn creates a positive feedback loop that drives the dramatic expansion of the PCM scaffold around mother centrioles during mitosis (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the mutual dependence observed experimentally.

claim: Asl, DSpd-2, and Cnn can all co-immunoprecipitate with one another in fly embryo extracts.
source: Although, we have identified direct interactions between Asl and DSpd-2 and between DSpd-2 and Cnn by Y2H, and the endogenous proteins can all co-immunoprecipitate with one another in fly embryo extracts (Conduit et al., 2010; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The requirement for Asl to initiate the mitotic recruitment of DSpd-2 and Cnn probably explains why these proteins are specifically recruited to mother centrioles.
source: The requirement for Asl to initiate the mitotic recruitment of DSpd-2 and Cnn probably explains why these proteins are specifically recruited to mother centrioles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Asl is specific to mother centrioles and initiates recruitment.

claim: Asl is not incorporated into daughter centrioles until they have passed through mitosis and matured into new mother centrioles.
source: We recently showed that although Asl is essential for centriole duplication, it is not incorporated into daughter centrioles until they have passed through mitosis and matured into new mother centrioles (Novak et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Asl/Cep152 proteins mainly localize to mother centrioles in several species.
source: and Asl/Cep152 proteins mainly localize to mother centrioles in several species (Sir et al., 2011; Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PCM appears to be preferentially associated with mother centrioles in many systems.
source: The PCM appears to be preferentially associated with mother centrioles in many systems (Piel et al., 2000; Conduit et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All mitotic PCM may be organized exclusively by mother centrioles.
source: Our findings provide a potential explanation for why this is so, and raise the intriguing possibility that all mitotic PCM may be organized exclusively by mother centrioles.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility raised based on the findings.

claim: There must be an alternative recruiter of Cnn besides DSpd-2, as the centrosomal localization of Cnn is not abolished in the absence of DSpd-2.
source: Although DSpd-2 seems to be the major recruiter of centrosomal Cnn in embryos, there must be an alternative recruiter, as the centrosomal localization of Cnn is not abolished in the absence of DSpd-2 (Figure 7, Figure 9C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some Cnn remains at centrosomes without DSpd-2.

claim: Asl is an attractive candidate as an alternative recruiter of Cnn.
source: Asl is an attractive candidate as anti-Asl antibodies perturb Cnn recruitment to centrioles (Conduit et al., 2010) (although this could be an indirect consequence of their effect on DSpd-2 recruitment), and Asl and Cnn interact in our Y2H analysis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on antibody effects and Y2H data.

claim: Human Cep152/Asl has a role in the centrosomal recruitment of human Cdk5Rap2/Cnn.
source: Moreover, human Cep152/Asl has a role in the centrosomal recruitment of human Cdk5Rap2/Cnn (Firat-Karalar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of DSpd-2, Cnn levels are reduced by only approximately 35% in brains but by approximately 80% in eggs.
source: Interestingly, in flies this alternative pathway appears to be stronger in larval brain cells than in eggs/embryos: in the absence of DSpd-2, Cnn levels are reduced by only ∼35% in brains (Figure 9C) but by ∼80% in eggs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from different cell types shown in Figures 7 and 9.

claim: The detail of mitotic PCM assembly pathway may vary between different cell types even in the same species.
source: Thus, the detail of mitotic PCM assembly pathway may vary between different cell types even in the same species.
evidence: This is inferred from the different dependencies observed in eggs versus brains.

claim: After DSpd-2 and Cnn have been recruited to centrioles, they rapidly assemble into scaffolds that then move slowly away from the centrioles.
source: Our data suggest that after DSpd-2 and Cnn have been recruited to centrioles, they rapidly assemble into scaffolds that then move slowly away from the centrioles.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP and 3D-SIM data throughout the manuscript.

claim: For Cnn, there is strong data indicating that scaffold assembly is regulated by phosphorylation.
source: For Cnn, there is strong data indicating that scaffold assembly is regulated by phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by previous work on Cnn phosphorylation.

claim: Cnn contains a phospho-regulated multimerization (PReM) domain that is phosphorylated by Polo/Plk1 in vitro and at centrosomes during mitosis in vivo.
source: Cnn contains a phospho-regulated multimerization (PReM) domain that is phosphorylated by Polo/Plk1 in vitro and at centrosomes during mitosis in vivo (Dobbelaere et al., 2008; Conduit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mimicking phosphorylation allows the PReM domain to multimerize in vitro and Cnn to spontaneously assemble into cytosolic scaffolds in vivo that can organize MTs.
source: Mimicking phosphorylation allows the PReM domain to multimerize in vitro and Cnn to spontaneously assemble into cytosolic scaffolds in vivo that can organize MTs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Conduit et al., 2014).

claim: Ablating phosphorylation does not interfere with Cnn recruitment to centrioles, but inhibits Cnn scaffold assembly.
source: Conversely, ablating phosphorylation does not interfere with Cnn recruitment to centrioles, but inhibits Cnn scaffold assembly (Conduit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DSpd-2 can assemble into a scaffold and this assembly is regulated in vivo so that it only occurs around mother centrioles.
source: We speculate that, like Cnn, DSpd-2 can assemble into a scaffold and that this assembly is regulated in vivo so that it only occurs around mother centrioles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed behavior of DSpd-2.

claim: Both DSpd-2 and Cnn exhibit an unusual dynamic behaviour at centrosomes where they incorporate into the PCM from the inside out.
source: It is striking that both DSpd-2 and Cnn exhibit an unusual dynamic behaviour at centrosomes. Both proteins incorporate into the PCM from the inside out, and are in constant flux, as the molecules that move slowly outward away from the centrioles are replaced by newly incorporated molecules close to the centriole surface (see Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DSpd-2 and Cnn are in constant flux, as the molecules that move slowly outward away from the centrioles are replaced by newly incorporated molecules close to the centriole surface.
source: Both proteins incorporate into the PCM from the inside out, and are in constant flux, as the molecules that move slowly outward away from the centrioles are replaced by newly incorporated molecules close to the centriole surface (see Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data showing continuous incorporation and outward movement.

claim: Inside out assembly means that the events close to the centriole surface, rather than at the periphery of the PCM, can ultimately regulate mitotic PCM assembly.
source: This inside out assembly is likely to have important consequences, as it means that the events close to the centriole surface, rather than at the periphery of the PCM, can ultimately regulate mitotic PCM assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the inside-out assembly mechanism.

claim: Inside out assembly may be particularly important in cells where centrioles organise centrosomes of different sizes, as is the case in certain asymmetrically dividing stem/progenitor cells.
source: This may be particularly important in cells where centrioles organise centrosomes of different sizes, as is the case in certain asymmetrically dividing stem/progenitor cells (Lesage et al., 2010; Nigg and Stearns, 2011; Pelletier and Yamashita, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature on asymmetric division.

claim: Fly neural stem cells use centrosome size asymmetry to ensure robust asymmetric division.
source: Fly neural stem cells, for example, use centrosome size asymmetry to ensure robust asymmetric division (Rebollo et al., 2007; Rusan and Peifer, 2007; Januschke et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is strong evidence that new and old mother centrioles differentially regulate the rate of Cnn incorporation in fly neural stem cells.
source: and there is strong evidence that new and old mother centrioles differentially regulate the rate of Cnn incorporation in these cells (Conduit and Raff, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mutations in human Cdk5Rap2/Cnn have been implicated in microcephaly.
source: Moreover, mutations in human Cdk5Rap2/Cnn have been implicated in microcephaly (Bond et al., 2005), a pathology linked to a failure in neural progenitor cell proliferation, although the precise reason for this is unclear (Bond and Woods, 2006; Megraw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microcephaly is a pathology linked to a failure in neural progenitor cell proliferation.
source: Moreover, mutations in human Cdk5Rap2/Cnn have been implicated in microcephaly (Bond et al., 2005), a pathology linked to a failure in neural progenitor cell proliferation, although the precise reason for this is unclear (Bond and Woods, 2006; Megraw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other PCM components besides DSpd-2 and Cnn are likely to make important contributions to centrosome maturation.
source: Although DSpd-2 and Cnn have a major role in centrosome maturation, we stress that other PCM components are likely to make important contributions.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement acknowledging the complexity of the system.

claim: Pericentrin has been implicated in PCM recruitment in several systems.
source: Pericentrin, for example, has been implicated in PCM recruitment in several systems (Martinez-Campos et al., 2004; Zimmerman et al., 2004; Lee and Rhee, 2011; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Kim and Rhee, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The fly homologue of Pericentrin, D-PLP, forms ordered fibrils in cultured S2 cells that extend away from the centriole wall and support PCM assembly in interphase.
source: and the fly homologue, D-PLP, forms ordered fibrils in cultured S2 cells that extend away from the centriole wall and support PCM assembly in interphase (Mennella et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: D-PLP centriolar fibrils cannot explain how centrioles organize such a vastly expanded PCM matrix during mitosis.
source: These centriolar fibrils, however, cannot explain how centrioles organize such a vastly expanded PCM matrix during mitosis
evidence: This is inferred from the scale difference between interphase and mitotic PCM.

claim: D-PLP appears to have an important, but more minor, role in mitotic PCM assembly in vivo.
source: and D-PLP appears to have an important, but more minor, role in mitotic PCM assembly in vivo (Martinez-Campos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Proteins like D-PLP will help recruit other PCM proteins and help form structural links within the PCM, thus strengthening the mitotic PCM matrix.
source: Nevertheless, proteins like D-PLP will certainly help recruit other PCM proteins and help form structural links within the PCM, thus strengthening the mitotic PCM matrix.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of D-PLP based on its known properties.

claim: In flies, most proteins, including the PCM fraction of D-PLP, are recruited into the PCM by an underlying PCM scaffold.
source: The important distinction is that, in flies at least, most proteins, including the PCM fraction of D-PLP, are recruited into the PCM by an underlying PCM scaffold
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP behavior of D-PLP and other PCM proteins.

claim: In flies, DSpd-2 and Cnn appear to form the underlying PCM scaffold.
source: whereas DSpd-2 and Cnn appear to form this scaffold.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: Homologues of Asl, DSpd-2, and Cnn have been implicated in PCM assembly in many species.
source: Homologues of Asl, DSpd-2, and Cnn have been implicated in PCM assembly in many species (Pelletier et al., 2004; Gomez-Ferreria et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2008; Haren et al., 2009; Barr et al., 2010; Cizmecioglu et al., 2010; Hatch et al., 2010; Joukov et al., 2010; Decker et al., 2011; Kim and Rhee, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanism of mitotic PCM recruitment identified in flies may be conserved through evolution.
source: suggesting that the mechanism of mitotic PCM recruitment we identify here in flies may be conserved through evolution.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of the proteins involved.

claim: No PCM component has yet been shown to assemble from the inside out and to flux away from the centrioles in any system other than flies.
source: To our knowledge, however, no PCM component has yet been shown to assemble from the inside out and to flux away from the centrioles in any other system.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The unusual dynamic behaviour of an underlying mitotic PCM scaffold will prove to be a general feature of mitotic centrosome assembly in many systems.
source: Nevertheless, although the precise molecular details will likely vary from cell type to cell type and from species to species, we suspect that this unusual dynamic behaviour of an underlying mitotic PCM scaffold will prove to be a general feature of mitotic centrosome assembly in many systems.
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of the mechanism.
